questions.question: Which property does a hash table's hash function need that a cryptographic hash function provides but a table does not require?
options: Determinism within a process
Collision resistance against an adversary searching for any colliding pair
Speed in the tens of nanoseconds
Roughly uniform distribution over the keys actually seen
questions.explanation: A table needs determinism, speed, uniformity, and avalanche; it does not need collision resistance, which is a cryptographic property costing about 100x more. A table under attack needs unpredictability of the colliding set, which is weaker than collision resistance and is what keyed hashes like SipHash provide.

questions.question: Why does Java's String.hashCode make collisions cheap to find on purpose?
options: It truncates the computed hash to the low 16 bits, so only 65,536 distinct values can ever exist
It is a simple linear combination with no avalanche, so equal-hash blocks can be reasoned about and concatenated at will
It derives the value from the object's memory address, which an attacker can read directly off the heap
It inspects only the first character of the string and ignores the entire rest of the input text
questions.explanation: h = 31*h + c is linear with essentially no avalanche: one-character changes move the hash predictably, so colliding blocks combine and a large equal-hash set costs work proportional to its bit-length, not its size. The hash is a full 32 bits, uses no address, and reads every character; the weakness is the linear structure, not the width.

questions.question: A chaining hash map receives n keys that all hash to one bucket. What is the total cost to insert them, and why?
options: O(n), because each insert into the flooded bucket is still just a single constant-time array write
O(n log n), because the overfull bucket stays automatically balanced as a self-adjusting search tree
O(n^2), because insert number i must compare the new key against the i-1 keys already in that bucket
O(1) amortized, because the periodic table resize redistributes the colliding keys across new buckets
questions.explanation: To honour uniqueness, each insert compares the new key against every key already in its bucket; with all n in one bucket that is 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Resizing adds buckets but every key still shares the one, so it does not help. Treeifying the bin is what would bring a single bucket down to O(log n) per operation.

questions.question: Why is adding a random secret constant to String.hashCode (h = hashCode(x) + seed) not a real defence?
options: The secret seed value can be read directly out of the running process memory by a determined attacker
The differences between the keys that produce a collision are left unchanged by adding any constant offset
The addition overflows the signed 32-bit integer range and silently discards the secret seed on every call
The seed used would have to be widened to at least 128 bits before it could make any practical difference
questions.explanation: Collisions depend on differences between hashes; adding the same constant to every hash leaves all those differences identical, so every previously colliding pair still collides regardless of the seed. The seed must feed a function whose output is a pseudorandom function of the key (SipHash), which is why the industry fix replaced the function rather than offsetting it.

questions.question: How does drawing a hash function at random from a universal family at process startup restore expected O(1) against adversarial keys?
options: It makes the hash function fully collision-resistant, so that no two distinct keys can share a bucket at all
Any fixed pair collides with probability at most 1/m over the family, and the chosen function is a startup secret
It sorts every key into order before hashing them, so the resulting bucket chains are always kept balanced
It causes the backing table to grow far faster than before, so the load factor can never rise under the flood
questions.explanation: Universality guarantees that any fixed pair collides with probability at most 1/m averaged over the family; because the specific function is chosen from a secret at startup, the attacker cannot predict the colliding set and the keys spread as if random, giving expected chain length n/m. It is not collision resistance, does not sort, and is independent of table growth.

questions.question: You must deduplicate requests by card number (PAN) without storing the PAN in the clear. Why is a bare SHA-256 of the PAN the wrong map key?
options: SHA-256 is simply too slow to run on the key of every single incoming request at payment-gateway scale
A 16-digit PAN has about 10^16 values, so an unkeyed digest is brute-force reversible; use an HMAC keyed from a vault
SHA-256 produces far too many collisions when it is fed short fixed-length 16-digit numeric inputs like a PAN
A 256-bit SHA-256 output is simply too wide a value to be usable as a key in a standard hash-map structure
questions.explanation: The PAN space is small enough that any unkeyed digest is trivially reversible by hashing all candidates, so SHA-256 provides no confidentiality for a PAN. A keyed hash (HMAC-SHA-256) or a token with the secret held in a KMS is required; the concern here is confidentiality of the key, which is a different requirement from the CPU-DoS defence and uses a different kind of key.
